summary: Describes the problem of encrypting the Server Name Indication (SNI) field in TLS, which currently reveals the site a client is visiting. It lists known attacks, discusses the existing HTTP co-tenancy approach, and sets out requirements for future TLS-layer solutions.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8744 is a checklist for anyone trying to hide the name of the website a client is visiting inside a TLS handshake. It collects the attacks that broke earlier attempts and turns them into requirements, and it reviews the workaround most sites use today, sending the name in the HTTP request instead of the handshake.

questions: why is sni not encrypted in tls
what are the requirements for encrypted sni
what is the cut and paste attack on sni encryption
subtitle: What an encrypted server name has to survive, and why the current work-around is not enough.

tldr.problem: The Server Name Indication extension tells a server which site a client wants, and it travels in cleartext, so it has become the last place an observer can read the name of the service being used.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the attacks that have killed earlier proposals, from copying an encrypted name to another connection through to shared secrets, denial of service, detectability, forward secrecy and fronting-server spoofing, and turns them into requirements.
tldr.outcome: The RFC does not design a scheme. It says that HTTP-level fronting meets only some of the requirements, that no scheme may meet all of them, and that the requirement to be undetectable may have to be dropped.

today: RFC 8744 is an Informational document from July 2020 that no RFC obsoletes or updates. It sets out requirements rather than a design, so the scheme it evaluates still has to be written and reviewed separately.

sections.title: Why the Server Name Became a Privacy Problem
sections.content:
Adversaries have historically monitored the use of web services through three channels: DNS requests, IP addresses in packet headers, and the data stream between user and services. Those channels are closing. A growing fraction of Internet communication is encrypted, mostly with TLS. DNS over TLS and DNS over HTTPS mitigate the disclosure of DNS information. More and more services are colocated on multiplexed servers, loosening the relation between an IP address and a web service. In virtual hosting, multiple services are hosted as co-tenants on one server, so the IP address and port do not uniquely identify a service. In cloud or Content Delivery Network solutions, one platform hosts the services of many organizations, and looking up which netblock an address belongs to reveals little.

Multiplexed servers rely on the Server Name Information (SNI) TLS extension to direct connections to the right service implementation, and this protocol element is transmitted in cleartext. As the other methods of monitoring get blocked, monitoring focuses on the cleartext SNI. The purpose of SNI encryption is to prevent that and to aid privacy.

Replacing cleartext SNI transmission with an encrypted variant would improve the privacy and reliability of TLS connections, but designing a proper solution is difficult. Several attempts at defining SNI encryption have been made, and they have generally floundered because the simple designs fail to mitigate several of the attacks the RFC collects. In the absence of a TLS-level solution, the most popular approach to SNI privacy for web services is HTTP-level fronting.

This document does not present the design of a solution. It provides guidelines for evaluating proposed solutions, and its review of HTTP-level solutions is not an endorsement of them.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption, private DNS and shared hosting have closed the usual ways to see what a client is doing. What is left is the name the client asks for at the start of the TLS handshake, which anyone on the path can read. Hiding it is worth doing, but the obvious designs have all failed in public.

sections.title: How an Extension for Servers Became a Tracking Signal
sections.content:
The SNI extension was specified in 2003 in RFC 3546 to facilitate management of colocation servers, in which multiple services shared the same IP address, for example multiple websites served by the same web server. The extension carries the name of a specific server, enabling the TLS connection to be established with the desired server context. The specification allowed different types of server names, but only the hostname variant was specified and deployed, and the extension is carried in cleartext in the TLS ClientHello message. The current specification is RFC 6066.

The SNI was defined to make servers easier to manage, but middlebox developers found they could use the information. Uses reviewed in RFC 8404 and raised during the writing of this document include filtering or censoring specific services; content filtering by network operators or ISPs, for example to implement parental controls or to block phishing sites; ISPs assigning different quality of service profiles to target services; enterprise firewalls blocking websites not deemed appropriate for work; and enterprise firewalls exempting specific websites from man-in-the-middle inspection, such as healthcare or financial sites where inspection would intrude on employee privacy. The SNI is probably also collected as part of the general metadata gathered by pervasive surveillance actors, for example to identify the services used by surveillance targets.

The cleartext SNI was not flagged as a problem in the Security Considerations sections of RFC 3546, RFC 4366 or RFC 6066, because those specifications did not anticipate this alternative usage. One reason may be that when they were written the same information was available through other means, such as tracking IP addresses, DNS names or server certificates. Many deployments still allocate different IP addresses to different services, but CDNs commonly serve a large number of services through a comparatively small number of addresses. The SNI carries the domain name of the server, which is also sent in DNS queries, so most of the uses above could equally be implemented by monitoring DNS traffic, but that is changing as resolvers adopt DNS over TLS and DNS over HTTPS.

The subjectAltName extension of type dNSName in the server certificate, or the common name component in its absence, exposes the same name as the SNI. In TLS 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2 servers send certificates in cleartext, so hiding the SNI alone bought little. In TLS 1.3 the server certificate is encrypted in transit, although encryption alone is insufficient to protect it.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension was added in 2003 so that one server could host many websites. It was not treated as sensitive at the time, partly because the same information leaked elsewhere. Now that the other leaks have been closed, the name in the handshake is the most convenient remaining one, and networks use it to block, rank or filter traffic.

sections.title: What an SNI Encryption Scheme Must Survive
sections.content:
Over the years there have been many proposals to add an SNI encryption option to TLS. A review of the TLS mailing list archives shows that many looked promising but were rejected after security reviews identified plausible attacks. The RFC collects those known attacks and turns them into requirements.

The simplest designs replace the cleartext SNI in the initial exchange with an encrypted value under a key known to the multiplexed server. Regardless of the encryption used, these designs can be broken by a cut-and-paste attack: the user starts a TLS connection including an encrypted SNI value; the adversary observes the exchange and copies the encrypted parameter; the adversary starts its own connection to the same server including the copied value; the server establishes the connection to the protected service, which sends its certificate, revealing the identity of the service. So the requirement is to mitigate cut-and-paste attacks.

Symmetric schemes that encrypt or hash the SNI with a shared secret are fragile, because the secret must be known by the multiplexed server and by every user of the protected services, so the compromise of a single user compromises the whole set. Encrypting the SNI may also create extra load for the server, because adversaries can mount denial-of-service attacks by generating random encrypted values and forcing useless decryption attempts; in many cases that decryption has to happen in a front-end component with limited resources while the TLS operations run elsewhere, so SNI-based denial of service could target the front end.

Some designs are also easy to spot. If handshakes using SNI encryption can be told apart from regular handshakes, for example because they carry specific extensions or specific cleartext SNI values, adversaries can block the feature or flag its users for special treatment. In the future a large fraction of handshakes might use SNI encryption, which would make detection a lesser concern, but near term only a small fraction can be assumed to use it.

Forward secrecy has to be maintained as well. TLS 1.3 is designed to provide it, so keys used in past sessions are not compromised even if the server's private key is. Designs that rely on the multiplexed server's public key to define the SNI encryption key fail this: if that private key is later compromised, adversaries can process archival records of past connections and retrieve the protected SNI.

Finally, solutions must support multi-party security contexts, where a fronting service relays to the protected service. In one class of solutions the client performs a single TLS handshake with the fronting service and verifies only the fronting service's certificate, which exposes the client to a man-in-the-middle attack by that fronting service. In another class the client verifies the protected service's certificate, which protects against that attack but leaves the client unable to verify the fronting service, enabling fronting server spoofing.
sections.plainLanguage: Each of these requirements comes from a way a proposed scheme has been broken. The encrypted name must not be replayable onto another connection, must not depend on a secret shared with every user, must not let an attacker overload the server with junk, must not be obvious to detect, must stay secret even if the server's key is later stolen, and must not leave the client unable to tell a real fronting server from a fake one.

sections.title: Protocol Coverage and the ALPN Question
sections.content:
The SNI encryption requirement does not stop with HTTP over TLS. Other applications use TLS too, including SMTP, DNS, IMAP and the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol, and they will benefit from SNI encryption as well. HTTP-only methods would not apply there. Even for the HTTPS case, the HTTPS tunneling service described in the RFC interacts awkwardly with the multiple streams feature of HTTP/2. This points to the need for an application-agnostic solution implemented fully in the TLS layer.

The Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) parameters of TLS let implementations negotiate the application-layer protocol used on a connection, and TLS provides them in cleartext during the initial handshake. Exposing the ALPN does not create the same privacy issues as exposing the SNI, but there is still a risk: some networks may block applications they do not understand, or that they wish users would not use. ALPN filtering could be very similar to the filtering of specific port numbers exposed in some networks, which has given rise to evasion tactics in which various protocols are tunneled over HTTP to use open ports 80 or 443. Filtering by ALPN would probably produce the same response, with applications moving over HTTP and only the HTTP ALPN values used, which they would not need to do if the ALPN were hidden the same way as the SNI.

Hiding the ALPN as well as the SNI is therefore desirable, but it implies engineering trade-offs: using the same technique for both may result in excess complexity, and it might be preferable to encrypt them independently.

The TLS handshake is also used over transports other than TCP, such as UDP with both DTLS and QUIC, and the requirement to encrypt the SNI applies just as well there. This points to a requirement for SNI encryption mechanisms to be applicable to non-TCP transports such as DTLS or QUIC.
sections.plainLanguage: A scheme that only hides the name for web traffic is of limited use, because email, name resolution and chat also run over TLS. The same goes for the protocol name the client asks for in the handshake, which is also readable. And TLS now runs over QUIC and DTLS as well as TCP, so any mechanism has to work there too.

sections.title: Domain Fronting, the Practice Used Today
sections.content:
In the absence of TLS-level SNI encryption, many sites rely on an HTTP co-tenancy solution, often called domain fronting. The TLS connection is established with the fronting server, and HTTP requests are then sent over that connection to the hidden service. The TLS SNI could be set to "fronting.example.com", the fronting server, while HTTP requests sent over that connection are directed to "hidden.example.com". The solution works well in practice when the fronting server and the hidden server are co-tenants of the same multiplexed server, and it can be deployed without modification to TLS and without requiring any specific version of TLS.

There are, however, issues with discovery, client implementations, trust and applicability. The client has to discover that the hidden service can be reached through the fronting server. The browser has to be directed to access the hidden service through the fronting service, a problem that was solved in the domain fronting experiment by implementing it as a pluggable transport for the Tor browser. Since the TLS connection is established with the fronting service, the client has no cryptographic proof that the content really comes from the hidden service, so the solution does not mitigate the context sharing issues described earlier. And since it is an HTTP-level solution, it does not protect non-HTTP protocols.

The trust issue is addressed by HTTPS-in-HTTPS tunneling, which treats the fronting server as an HTTP proxy: the client establishes a TLS connection to the fronting server and then issues an HTTP connect request to the hidden server, establishing an end-to-end HTTPS-over-TLS connection between the client and the hidden server. This requires double encryption of every packet and requires the fronting server to decrypt and relay messages, which makes the implementation onerous.

Clients would see their privacy compromised if they contacted the wrong fronting server, because that server could disclose their access to adversaries. This requires a controlled way to indicate which fronting server is acceptable to the hidden service. The problem is similar to the word-of-mouth variant of the fronting server spoofing attack, where fake advice is distributed such as telling people to use fake.example.com as the fronting server for hidden.example.com. In practice the attack is well mitigated when the hidden service is reached through a specialized application, because the fronting server's name can be programmed into that application, but it is harder to mitigate when a general-purpose web browser is used. Proposed solutions include a special form of certificate codifying the relation between the fronting and hidden server, and obtaining the relation through DNS, possibly using DNSSEC. CDNs have a similar requirement, since they must convince the client that www.example.com can be reached through cdn-node-xyz.example.net, and most have deployed DNS-based solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: The workaround in use today is to hide the real destination in the HTTP request instead of in the handshake. The handshake names a well-known site, and the request inside it names the site that is really wanted. It needs no change to TLS, but the client can no longer check cryptographically that it is talking to the site it asked for, and it only works for web traffic.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists the attacks against SNI encryption and presents the requirements to mitigate them. Current HTTP-based solutions meet only some of these requirements. In practice, it may well be that no solution can meet every requirement and that practical solutions will have to make some compromises. In particular, the requirement to not stick out may have to be lifted, especially for proposed solutions that could quickly reach large-scale deployments.

Replacing cleartext SNI transmission by an encrypted variant will break or reduce the efficacy of the operational practices implemented in middleboxes, such as filtering specific services and applying different quality of service to them. Alternative solutions will have to be developed for those functions, for example DNS providers offering customers the option to opt in to filtering services for parental control and phishing protection, and per-stream quality of service provided by a combination of packet marking and end-to-end agreements.
sections.plainLanguage: The requirements may not all be satisfiable at once, and the RFC expects that at least one of them, being untraceable in use, may have to go. It also accepts that hiding the name will break network filtering, and that enterprises will have to move that filtering to the DNS resolver or to software on the user's own machine.

messages.label: COPY THE ENCRYPTED SNI
messages.note: The adversary observes the exchange and copies the encrypted SNI parameter.

messages.label: TLS CONNECTION
messages.note: The copied encrypted SNI is replayed in the adversary's own connection.

messages.label: CERTIFICATE
messages.note: The protected service sends its certificate, revealing the identity of the service.

viz.caption: THE REQUIREMENTS A PROPOSED SCHEME MUST MEET

items.title: Mitigate cut-and-paste
items.text: An encrypted name copied from one connection must not reveal the service on another.

items.title: Avoid widely shared secrets
items.text: A secret held by the server and every user would fall with one compromised user.

items.title: Prevent SNI-based denial of service
items.text: Random encrypted names must not force the server into useless decryption work.

items.title: Do not stick out
items.text: The handshake must not be easy to tell apart from an ordinary one.

items.title: Maintain forward secrecy
items.text: Past connections stay protected even if the server's key is later compromised.

items.title: Multi-party security context
items.text: The client must be able to authenticate the real service even when a fronting server is in between.
